blocks.text: 1. Grid Search

blocks.alt: Hyperparameters form a full grid, trying every combination

blocks.text: The Cross Validation module, just completed, built the entire machinery needed to honestly, reliably measure how well any one specific model, with any one specific hyperparameter setting, actually performs. The Hyperparameter Tuning module now turns to the natural next question that machinery makes possible: given many candidate hyperparameter settings to choose from, which one should actually get selected in the first place?

Grid Search is the simplest, most exhaustive answer to this question, and it has already appeared directly in this course, since GridSearchCV was used explicitly in the Nested Cross Validation topic's worked example, without yet receiving its own full, dedicated explanation. This topic gives Grid Search that complete treatment, covering exactly how it works, what it guarantees, and precisely where its exhaustive approach starts to become impractical.
2. Building the Grid

blocks.alt: Parameter A values and parameter B values together build the grid

blocks.text: Grid Search begins by requiring a fixed, explicit list of candidate values to be chosen for every single hyperparameter being tuned. For an SVM classifier, exactly the algorithm already covered in depth in the Classification module, this might mean choosing candidate values like 0.1, 1, and 10 for the regularization parameter C, and separately choosing candidate values like 0.01, 0.1, and 1 for the kernel parameter gamma.

Grid Search then forms every possible combination across all of these hyperparameters together, constructing what is literally a full grid of candidate settings. With 3 candidate values for C and 3 candidate values for gamma, this produces 3 times 3, or 9, total distinct combinations, each one representing one complete, specific hyperparameter setting that will actually get evaluated.
3. The Exhaustive Search Process

blocks.alt: Every combination gets cross validated to find the best combination

blocks.text: Once the full grid of combinations has been constructed, Grid Search proceeds by evaluating every single combination in that grid, one at a time, with no combination skipped. Each combination is evaluated using cross validation, exactly the K-Fold machinery already covered in depth throughout the previous module, producing an average cross validation score for that specific combination.

This process repeats for every remaining combination in the grid, and once every single one has been evaluated this way, Grid Search simply selects whichever combination achieved the best average cross validation score across the entire grid. This exhaustive, leave-nothing-untried approach is precisely what gives Grid Search its name and its defining character.
4. Built Directly on the Cross Validation Module

It is worth being explicit about a connection this topic has been building toward since its opening section. Grid Search is not a standalone technique that happens to also use cross validation; it is built directly, structurally, on top of the entire Cross Validation module's foundation, specifically relying on K-Fold Cross Validation to evaluate every single combination in its grid fairly and reliably.

Furthermore, reporting a genuinely honest final performance number after Grid Search has selected its best combination requires exactly the Nested Cross Validation structure already covered in the previous module's closing topic, since using the same cross validation loop both to select the best grid combination and to report that combination's final score would reintroduce precisely the optimistic bias Nested Cross Validation was built to eliminate.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Reporting GridSearchCV's own best_score_ directly as a model's final expected performance repeats exactly the naive single-loop tuning mistake already covered in depth in the Nested Cross Validation topic. A separate, genuinely honest outer evaluation loop is still needed for a trustworthy final number.

blocks.text: 5. A Genuine Guarantee, With a Real Limit

blocks.alt: Grid search finds the best within the grid, but is limited to what's in the grid

blocks.text: Grid Search offers one genuine, mathematically solid guarantee: because it checks literally every single combination defined within the grid, it is guaranteed to find whichever combination, among those actually included in the grid, performs best according to the cross validation evaluation used. There is no randomness, no chance of missing a combination that was genuinely part of the search space.

This guarantee comes with an important, easy-to-overlook limit, however: it applies only to combinations actually included in the grid, not to the true, best possible hyperparameter setting overall. If the genuinely optimal value for C happens to be 5, but the grid only included candidate values of 0.1, 1, and 10, Grid Search will never find or even consider that true optimum, no matter how exhaustively it searches within the grid it was actually given.
6. The Combinatorial Explosion Problem

blocks.alt: Many parameters bring a combinatorial explosion

blocks.text: Grid Search's exhaustive approach runs directly into a serious scaling problem as more hyperparameters get added to the search. With 2 hyperparameters and 3 candidate values each, the grid contains a perfectly manageable 9 combinations, exactly the example already covered earlier in this topic. With 4 hyperparameters and 5 candidate values each, the grid balloons to 625 combinations.

With 6 hyperparameters and 10 candidate values each, the grid reaches a full 1,000,000 combinations, and every single one of those combinations requires its own complete cross validation run underneath it. This combinatorial explosion, the grid size growing multiplicatively, and effectively exponentially, with every additional hyperparameter or additional candidate value added, is Grid Search's single most serious practical limitation, and it is precisely what motivates Random Search, the very next topic in this module.
7. The Real Computational Cost

The total computational cost of Grid Search is the total number of grid combinations, multiplied by K, the number of cross validation folds used to evaluate each individual combination. A grid of 100 combinations, evaluated with standard 5-fold cross validation, requires 100 times 5, or 500, total individual model training runs to complete.

Every additional hyperparameter added to the search, or every additional candidate value added for an existing hyperparameter, multiplies this already substantial cost directly, exactly the combinatorial explosion already covered in the previous section. This direct, multiplicative relationship between grid size and total computational cost is why Grid Search, despite its clean guarantee and simple logic, quickly becomes impractical on anything beyond a genuinely small hyperparameter search space.
8. When Grid Search Is the Right Choice

blocks.alt: A small search space points toward using grid search

blocks.text: Grid Search remains a genuinely sensible, practical choice specifically when tuning very few hyperparameters, typically one to three, since the resulting grid stays small enough to search exhaustively without incurring excessive computational cost, exactly the manageable end of the combinatorial explosion already covered in this topic.

It is also the right choice whenever a guaranteed, fully reproducible, exhaustive result over a genuinely small search space matters more than raw efficiency, since Grid Search involves no randomness at all, meaning the exact same grid, run on the exact same data, always produces the exact same result, a property some workflows, particularly ones requiring strict reproducibility, genuinely value. When facing many hyperparameters, or a wide range of candidate values for even a few hyperparameters, Grid Search becomes computationally infeasible, and Random Search or Bayesian Optimization, both covered in the next two topics, become the more practical choices instead.

blocks.text: 9. A Preview: Choosing the Grid Values Themselves

Beyond deciding which hyperparameters to tune at all, choosing exactly which candidate values to include in the grid for each one is itself a meaningful, consequential decision worth previewing here. Linear spacing, evenly spaced candidate values like 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, works well for hyperparameters that behave roughly linearly across their reasonable range.

Log spacing, values spaced evenly on a logarithmic scale instead, like 0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, and 10, works far better for hyperparameters that naturally span several orders of magnitude, regularization strength being a classic example already encountered throughout the Regression and Classification modules. Choosing the right spacing strategy for each specific hyperparameter, and more generally designing the search space itself well, is covered in its own full, dedicated depth in the Hyperparameter Spaces topic, closing out this module.
10. Worked Example
The example below runs Grid Search over an SVM classifier's C and gamma hyperparameters, directly illustrating the grid construction and total combination count covered throughout this topic.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X = rng.normal(size=(200, 4))
y = (X[:, 0] + X[:, 1] * 0.5 + rng.normal(scale=0.5, size=200) > 0).astype(int)

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.3, random_state=42)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_train_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)

param_grid = {
    'C': [0.1, 1, 10],
    'gamma': [0.01, 0.1, 1],
}
print(f"Total grid combinations: {len(param_grid['C']) * len(param_grid['gamma'])}")

grid_search = GridSearchCV(SVC(kernel='rbf'), param_grid, cv=5, return_train_score=False)
grid_search.fit(X_train_scaled, y_train)

print(f"Best combination found: {grid_search.best_params_}")
print(f"Best cross validation score: {grid_search.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"Test set score with best combination: {grid_search.score(X_test_scaled, y_test):.3f}")

results = grid_search.cv_results_
print(f"\nTotal combinations actually evaluated: {len(results['params'])}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The gap between grid_search.best_score_ and the true test set score is worth watching directly; a large gap can indicate the naive single-loop leakage covered in this topic's warning note, since best_score_ was selected for rather than independently measured.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Grid Search exhaustively evaluates every combination of predefined candidate hyperparameter values using cross validation.
It is built directly on the Cross Validation module's foundation, relying on K-Fold for evaluation and Nested CV for honest reporting.
It guarantees finding the best combination within the grid, but can never find a good value outside the grid it was given.
Grid size grows multiplicatively with every added hyperparameter or candidate value, a combinatorial explosion.
Total cost equals the number of grid combinations times the number of cross validation folds per combination.
It suits very few hyperparameters, typically one to three, or situations where guaranteed reproducibility matters.
It becomes computationally infeasible with many hyperparameters or wide candidate ranges, motivating the next topic.
Choosing linear versus log spacing for candidate values is itself a meaningful decision, covered fully later in this module.
Next up: Random Search, which samples combinations randomly instead of exhaustively, scaling far better to larger search spaces.
